comment: The system's claim is missing (it only provided a comma: ,). Since there is no substantive claim to evaluate against the passage discussing the undisclosed use of plexiglass, it cannot be supported.

The passage establishes the facts of the case, noting that the wrong pipe was used and that fixing it would mean 'the demolition at great expense of substantial parts of the completed structure'. However, the passage ends at the refusal of the certificate and the initiation of the suit. It never explicitly states the legal conclusion that this was a 'trivial defect' or that it 'did not defeat substantial performance.'

The passage directly states that the statute 'by its own words and as applied, purports to punish mere advocacy and to forbid, on pain of criminal punishment, assembly with others merely to advocate the described type of action' and concludes that 'Such a statute falls within the condemnation of the First and Fourteenth Amendments'.

The text confirms that when a corporation exercises the privilege of conducting activities in a state, it enjoys the benefits and protections of those laws. It further supports the claim by stating these activities give rise to obligations, and requiring the corporation to respond to a suit to enforce them is not undue.

The passage states exactly what the system claims: the Court agreed the respondent proved a prima facie case, that the petitioner sought mechanics (the respondent's trade) after his rejection, and that the petitioner did not dispute the respondent's qualifications, acknowledging his past work was 'satisfactory'.

The provided text explicitly matches the claim, outlining the question of whether Title VII prohibits requiring a high school education or passing a general intelligence test when (a) they aren't significantly related to successful job performance, (b) they disqualify Negroes at a higher rate, and (c) the jobs were formerly filled only by white employees due to a longstanding preference.
Similar to Check 1, the system's claim is merely a comma (,). There is no claim text to verify against the passage detailing the objective of Title VII.

The text directly mirrors the claim, stating that while an antiharassment policy isn't necessary in every instance as a matter of law, it can be addressed when litigating the first element. It also notes that an unreasonable failure to use a provided complaint procedure will normally satisfy the employer's burden under the second element.
The passage includes the exact quote cited in the claim about a sense of inferiority affecting the motivation of a child to learn and retarding educational and mental development.
The system's claim is missing (,). Without a claim to evaluate, it cannot be supported by the passage.

While the passage discusses the 'Rapid Shave' commercial and the 'sandpaper test', it cuts off right after stating that 'Rapid Shave was applied to a substance that appeared to be sandpaper, and immediately thereafter a razor was shown shaving the substance clean'. The provided passage never mentions the crucial detail that it was actually an undisclosed mock-up or plexiglass.

The passage directly states the purpose was to make certain that 'in all matters except those in which some federal law is controlling, the federal courts... would apply as their rules of decision the law of the State, unwritten as well as written'.

The passage only outlines the arguments of the two parties. It notes Erie's contention that Pennsylvania law should apply to longitudinal pathways and Tompkins' contention that 'general law' should apply. The text does not contain the Court's final holding that the federal court was 'not free to disregard' the state rule.

The passage directly quotes the rejected earlier approach about federal courts assuming the power to declare rules of decision in the broad field of general law, and notes that the previous construction giving them this power was erroneous.

The text explicitly states that where employers have instituted employment tests and qualifications with an exclusionary effect on minority applicants, such requirements must be shown to bear a demonstrable relationship to successful performance of the jobs.
